1           PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that on October 3, 2025 at 10:00 am, or as soon thereafter as the

2    matter may be heard, in Courtroom 6, 450 Golden Gate Avenue, San Francisco, California 94102,

3    defendant Meta Platforms, Inc.1 will and hereby does move the Court for an order dismissing with

4    prejudice the complaint (“Compl.”), Dkt. No. 1, filed by plaintiff, pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6) of the

5    Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. This motion is based on this Notice of Motion, the supporting

6    Memorandum of Points and Authorities, other materials in the record, argument of counsel, and

7    such other matters as the Court may consider.

8                                       STATEMENT OF ISSUES

9           1.      Whether all of plaintiff’s claims should be dismissed as time-barred, given that all

10   of them are subject to a four-year statute of limitations and the complaint is devoid of factual

11   allegations that Facebook did anything allegedly unlawful within the last seven years.

12          2.      Whether plaintiff’s breach of contract claim should be dismissed, given that plain-

13   tiff does not identify any contractual provision that Facebook supposedly breached and does not

14   make any factual allegations showing that it was injured due to Facebook’s purported breach of

15   contract.

16          3.      Whether plaintiff’s claims for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair

17   dealing, violation of the California Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”), and unjust enrichment—all

18   of which rely on the same factual allegations and seek the same damages as plaintiff’s breach of

19   contract claim—should be dismissed for the same reasons as the breach of contract claim, in ad-

20   dition to further reasons specific to those claims.

1                                    SUMMARY OF ARGUMENTS2

2            Plaintiff’s threadbare complaint is devoid of factual allegations that would support its

3    claims. All of plaintiff’s claims are predicated on the assertion that starting over a decade ago and

4    going until 2017, Facebook supposedly used a “blended price” auction methodology rather than a

5    “second price” auction process that plaintiff says Facebook was required to use instead. Plaintiff’s

6    breach of contract claim is fatally flawed because plaintiff does not and cannot allege that the

7    purported contract between the parties promised anything about the particular auction methodol-

8    ogy that Facebook would use, let alone that the company would use a “second price” auction pro-

9    cess. Plaintiff’s remaining claims are all based on the same core theory—that Facebook somehow

10   acted wrongfully by using the “blended price” process—but fail to show why using such a process

11   would give rise to any legally cognizable claim. Plaintiff’s claim that it and other advertisers were

12   “overcharged” rests on the assumption that Facebook promised to use the “second price” process

13   rather than the “blended price” process that it allegedly used. But because there was no such

14   promise or requirement to use a specific auction methodology, even if Facebook did use the

15   “blended price” process, the amounts it charged advertisers were not “overcharges”—they were

16   simply the amounts determined by an auction process that Facebook was not prohibited (contrac-

17   tually or otherwise) from employing. The complaint should be dismissed for this reason and as

18   further explained below.

19           First, all of plaintiff’s claims are time-barred. California law imposes a four-year statute

20   of limitations on claims sounding in contract as well as claims under the UCL. According to the

21   complaint, Facebook changed its auction process in 2013 and again in late 2017. The complaint

22   lacks any factual allegations that Facebook engaged in any wrongdoing after 2017—nearly eight

23   years before plaintiff filed its complaint. The complaint is time-barred on its face. See, e.g., In re

24   Tesla Advanced Driver Assistance Sys. Litig., 2023 WL 6391477, at *9 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 30, 2023);

25   Wen v. Greenpoint Mortg. Funding, Inc., 2021 WL 5449048, at *3–4 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 22, 2021).

26

27

28   2

         ets, citations, and footnotes have been omitted.

1           Second, even if the Court were to overlook plaintiff’s untimeliness, the complaint fails to

2    allege any breach of contract. The sole agreement that plaintiff allegedly entered with Facebook

3    says nothing about which auction mechanism Facebook would use and does not provide any prom-

4    ises to advertisers about how auctions would work. Unable to point to any promise, plaintiff relies

5    on a contractual provision stating that “[t]he amount you owe will be calculated based on our

6    tracking mechanisms.” There are no allegations that Facebook deviated from its “tracking mech-

7    anisms” when calculating the amount that plaintiff or any other advertiser owed. And there are no

8    allegations that any contract required Facebook to use any particular kind of auction system, which

9    is fatal to plaintiff’s breach of contract claim. See, e.g., Hammerling v. Google LLC, 615 F. Supp.

10   3d 1069, 1095 (N.D. Cal. 2022) (Breyer, J.).

11          Third, plaintiff fails to plead any of its alternative theories of liability, which are based on

12   the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, unjust enrichment, and the UCL. Plaintiff

13   cannot use these causes of action to manufacture a promise that Facebook never made: it is neither

14   bad faith, nor unjust, nor unfair for Facebook to have used the “blended price” auction process it

15   is alleged to have used, given that it made no promises to users that it would use any particular

16   form of auction to price advertisements. See, e.g., Lewis v. Google LLC, 461 F. Supp. 3d 938, 961

17   (N.D. Cal. 2020), aff’d, 851 F. App’x 723 (9th Cir. 2021); Rosell v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 2014

18   WL 4063050, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 15, 2014).

19                         STATEMENT OF FACTS AND ALLEGATIONS 3

20          A. Facebook’s Use of an Auction System to Sell Advertisements

21          During the time period discussed in the complaint, Facebook generated revenue from sell-

22   ing advertising placements to advertisers. See Compl. ¶ 1–11, 15. Facebook used an auction

23   process to determine which advertisement to allocate to available ad slots. See id. ¶¶ 2, 16–33.

24   The auction process incorporated both ad- and user-specific factors, including the type of user that

25   the advertiser was trying to target, the advertiser’s desired interaction with the user (for instance,

1    whether the advertiser seeks “impressions,” “clicks,” or “conversions”), and the value to the user

2    of seeing the advertisement. Id. ¶¶ 18, 19, 24. Ultimately, Facebook’s auction process determined

3    the total value of each ad competing for a particular ad slot and selected the winning ad. Id. ¶¶ 25,

4    26. Facebook also used this auction process to determine the price that an advertiser would pay.

5    See id. ¶¶ 28, 29.

6           The complaint discusses two different auction processes, which differ based on how they

7    incorporate the winning monetary bid into the price that the winning bidder pays. In a “second

8    price” auction, “the winning ‘first’ bid is excluded and the winning bidder’s cost is the amount of

9    the second-highest bid.” Id. ¶ 2. In such auctions, “winning bids should not have been used in

10   calculating the price the winning advertiser would pay.” Id. ¶ 16; see id. ¶¶ 17, 29, 30. By contrast,

11   in a “blended price” auction (also referred to as a “weighted average” auction), “the cost charged

12   to the winning bidder was a blend of the highest ‘first’ bid and the second-highest bid.” Id. ¶ 2;

13   see also id. ¶ 29. Notably, the winning bidder necessarily pays less than their actual bid under

14   either of these auction processes. See id. ¶¶ 2, 29.

15          Plaintiff alleges that Facebook “purported to use” a “version of the ‘second price’ auction

16   process for pricing advertisements” during the relevant period. Id. ¶¶ 2, 16. But the complaint

17   does not cite any instance of Facebook “purport[ing]” to use such a process. Nor does it cite to

18   any provision of a contract or any written or oral representation made by Facebook to plaintiff (or

19   anyone else) promising to use a “second price” auction methodology for calculating winning bids.

20   Instead, the complaint cites a 2015 article in Wired magazine as well as two articles in journals

21   from 2014 and 2018 to support the allegation that Facebook used a “generalized second price

22   auction.” Id. ¶ 16; see also id. ¶ 56 (alleging, without citation, that it was “widely understood”

23   that Facebook used a “version of” a “second price auction”).

24          B. Facebook Allegedly Changed Its Auction Process

25          Plaintiff alleges that “Facebook engineers changed the auction process in a 2013 update to

26   the software code used to run Facebook’s advertisement auctions,” which resulted in Facebook

27   running a “blended price” auction. Id. ¶¶ 7, 34. Unlike a “second price” auction, a “blended price”

28   auction would incorporate the amount of the winning bid in the price and would result in

1     advertisers paying more than they would have paid in a “second price” auction. Id. ¶ 29. Plaintiff

2     alleges that the change from a “second price” auction to a “blended price” auction “caused a ma-

3     terial increase in advertising revenues” for Facebook. Id. ¶ 36.

4             According to plaintiff, Facebook investigated “pricing irregularities in its advertising auc-

5     tion process” in 2016. Id. ¶ 37. The complaint includes what purports to be an internal Facebook

6     document showing that “the price the advertisers paid [on Facebook] was correlated with their

7     bids.” Id. ¶ 41. Plaintiff alleges that Facebook engineers continued this research through the third

8     quarter of 2017. Id. ¶ 45. On or around September 2017, Facebook allegedly began implementing

9     a further change to its auction process. The complaint cites an internal email dated September 14,

10    2017, in which a Facebook employee allegedly wrote, “We agree on a (possibly slow) rollout

11    timeline,” and allegedly instructed his team to “[f]ind a way to do ‘slow’ rollout.” Id. ¶ 49. The

12    complaint alleges that Facebook “gradually expanded the change to 100% of users over a period

13    of time,” id. ¶ 50, but does not allege what was changed or when the alleged change was complete.

14            C. Alleged Agreements Between Facebook and Its Advertisers

15            Facebook uses written contracts to govern its relationships with advertisers. See id. ¶ 53.

16    During the time period discussed in the complaint, Facebook advertisers agreed to Facebook’s

17    Statement of Rights and Responsibilities (as it was formerly known), which provided, among other

18    things, that “You will pay for your Orders in accordance with our Payments Terms. The amount

19    you owe will be calculated based on our tracking mechanisms.” Id. Plaintiff alleges that the

20    Statement of Rights and Responsibilities incorporated a document titled Self-Service Ad Terms,

21    which also stated that “You will pay for your Orders in accordance with our Payments Terms. The

22    amount you owe will be calculated based on our tracking mechanisms.” Id. Neither document

23    discussed how Facebook priced advertisements, let alone its auction price methodology. See id.

24    ¶ 54.

25            The complaint also references other Facebook webpages, which are not alleged to be part

26    of the contract between Facebook and its advertisers. Plaintiff cites a page entitled “How ad billing

27    works on Facebook,” which allegedly stated that “[t]he pricing of Facebook ads is based on an

28    auction system where ads compete for impressions based on bid and performance.” Id. ¶ 55.

1     Plaintiff also cites a page entitled “About ad auctions”; the complaint does not quote any language

2     from this page, but states that “[t]hese webpages made clear that advertisements were to be priced

3     according to Facebook’s auction process.” Id. ¶ 56. Nothing further is alleged with respect to

4     auction processes.

5            D. Plaintiff’s Lawsuit

6            Plaintiff Iron Tribe Fitness is allegedly a fitness company that “advertised on Facebook

7     through its advertising auction process during the Class Period.” Id. ¶ 14. The complaint does

8     not include any allegations about when in the class period plaintiff advertised on Facebook, what

9     type of advertisements plaintiff ran, or how much plaintiff paid for any such advertisements.

10           Plaintiff purports to bring its complaint as a putative class action on behalf of itself and a

11    class consisting of “customers of Facebook that purchased advertisements during the period when

12    the 2013 coding change caused Facebook to overcharge advertising customers.” Id. ¶ 57. The

13    complaint defines the “Class Period” as the period during which “the 2013 coding change caused

14    Facebook to overcharge advertising customers,” but does not provide specific dates or an end date.

15    Id.

16           Based on the foregoing factual allegations, plaintiff asserts four claims. First, plaintiff

17    claims that Facebook breached its contract with advertisers, which allegedly consisted of the State-

18    ment of Rights and Responsibilities and the documents and webpages incorporated therein. Id.

19    ¶¶ 68–73. Second, plaintiff claims that Facebook breached the implied covenant of good faith and

20    fair dealing by overcharging and failing to reimburse the class. Id. ¶¶ 74–78. Third, plaintiff

21    claims that Facebook violated the “unfair” prong of the UCL. Id. ¶¶ 79–84. And fourth, plaintiff

22    claims that Facebook was unjustly enriched by its conduct. Id. ¶¶ 85–90.

23                                              ARGUMENT

24           Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), the Court may dismiss a complaint for

25    failure to state a claim upon which relief may be granted. To survive a motion to dismiss under

26    Rule 12(b)(6), “a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a

27    claim for relief that is plausible on its face.’” Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). “A

28    Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal can be based on the lack of a cognizable legal theory or the absence of

1     sufficient facts alleged under a cognizable legal theory.” Godecke v. Kinetic Concepts, Inc., 937

2     F.3d 1201, 1208 (9th Cir. 2019). The Court need not accept as true “allegations that are merely

3     conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences.” In re Gilead Scis. Sec.

4     Litig., 536 F.3d 1049, 1055 (9th Cir. 2008). “Threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of

5     action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice.” Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678. A plain-

6     tiff must allege “more than an unadorned, the-defendant-unlawfully-harmed-me accusation.” Id.

7     I.     This Action Is Time-Barred

8            Each of plaintiff’s claims is subject to a four-year statute of limitations. But the complaint

9     does not allege that Facebook engaged in any relevant—let alone wrongful—conduct later than

10    2017. As a result, the entire complaint is time-barred.

11           A four-year statute of limitations governs each of plaintiff’s claims. In California, breach

12    of contract claims are subject to a four-year statute of limitations. Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 337(a);

13    see Apple Inc. v. Allan & Assocs., 445 F. Supp. 3d 42, 58 (N.D. Cal. 2020). The same four-year

14    statute of limitations applies to plaintiff’s related claims for breach of the implied covenant of good

15    faith and fair dealing and unjust enrichment. See Fehl v. Manhattan Ins. Grp., 2012 WL 10047,

16    at *4 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 2, 2012) (“a four year statute of limitations applies” because claim for “breach

17    of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing sounds in contract”); Al-Ahmed v. Twitter, Inc., 648

18    F. Supp. 3d 1140, 1155 n.1 (N.D. Cal. 2023) (statute of limitations for unjust enrichment is “based

19    on the underlying wrong” and if “founded on a written contract, it is 4 years”). And claims under

20    the UCL “shall be commenced within four years after the cause of action accrued.” Cal. Bus. &

21    Prof. Code § 17208; see Van v. Language Line Servs., Inc., 2016 WL 3143951, at *30 (N.D. Cal.

22    June 6, 2016).

23           Under California law, the general rule is that the statute of limitations runs from the occur-

24    rence of the last element essential to the cause of action. Allan & Assocs., 445 F. Supp. 3d at 58.

25    Here, the complaint alleges that the putative misconduct ended almost eight years ago: it alleges

26    that on September 14, 2017, Facebook engineers were told to “rollout” a change that “corrected”

27    the supposedly wrongful auction process, and further alleges that Facebook “gradually expanded

28    the change to 100% of users.” Compl. ¶¶ 49, 50. The complaint does not allege that Facebook

21    II.     Plaintiff’s Breach of Contract Claim Should Be Dismissed Because Plaintiff Does

22            Not Allege that Facebook Breached Any Contract

23            Even if the Court concludes that plaintiff’s claims are not time-barred, plaintiff’s breach of

24    contract claim fails on the merits. (As do its other claims, for reasons set forth below.) To state a

25    claim for breach of contract, plaintiff must allege (1) the existence of a contract, (2) plaintiff’s

26    performance under the contract, (3) defendant’s breach, and (4) damage. Hammerling, 615 F.

27    Supp. 3d at 1094. Plaintiff’s breach of contract claim is subject to dismissal on multiple independ-

4               Plaintiff’s remaining claims fail for the same reasons as its breach of contract claim and/or

6               A.      Plaintiff’s Breach of Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing

7                       Claim Should Be Dismissed

8               Plaintiff’s claim for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing incorpo-

9     rates the failings of plaintiff’s contract claim and should be dismissed for similar reasons.

10              First, plaintiff cannot use the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing to enforce

11    obligations on Facebook that are inconsistent with the terms of the parties’ purported written con-

12    tract. The implied covenant “cannot impose substantive duties or limits on the contracting parties

13    beyond those incorporated in the specific terms of their agreement.” Guz v. Bechtel Nat’l, Inc., 24

14    Cal. 4th 317, 349–50 (2000). As a result, “to the extent a plaintiff seeks to impose limits ‘beyond

15    those to which the parties actually agreed, the [implied covenant] claim is invalid.’” Lewis, 461

16    F. Supp. 3d at 961 (quoting Guz, 24 Cal. 4th at 349), aff’d, 851 F. App’x 723 (9th Cir. 2021); see

17    also Bevis v. Terrace View Partners, LP, 33 Cal. App. 5th 230, 256–57 (Cal. 2019) (the implied

18    covenant of good faith and fair dealing “may not be ‘read to prohibit a party from doing that which

19    is expressly permitted by an agreement’”).

20              As discussed, the purported contract alleged in the complaint expressly permitted Facebook

21    to charge advertisers “in accordance with our Payments Terms” and “based on our tracking mech-

22    anisms.” Compl. ¶ 53. Moreover, nothing in the purported contract obligated Facebook to use a

23    particular auction process or reimburse advertisers for any differences in payment triggered by the

22           B.      Plaintiff’s UCL Claim Should Be Dismissed

23           Plaintiff’s lone statutory claim—for violation of the UCL—fares no better. Plaintiff brings

24    its UCL claim solely under the “unfair” prong of the statute. In doing so, plaintiff relies on the

25    same allegations that underlie its legally insufficient breach of contract claim, rendering its UCL

26    claim both duplicative and inadequate. In addition, plaintiff’s allegations do not meet any of the

27    standards that California courts have developed to evaluate “unfairness” under the UCL. For these

28    reasons, the UCL claim should also be dismissed.

1                First, plaintiff improperly repackages its breach of contract allegations in an attempt to

2     manufacture a cognizable violation of the UCL. But a breach of contract violates the UCL only if

3     a plaintiff alleges unfair conduct “independent of the breach” and includes “a ‘plus’ factor to make

4     it independently actionable.” Rosell, 2014 WL 4063050, at *6. “Otherwise, every garden-variety

5     breach of contract claim, which often includes the charge that the breach was ‘unfair’ to the non-

6     breaching party, would double as a UCL claim.” Id.; see also Santa Barbara Smokehouse, Inc. v.

7     Aquachile, Inc., 2020 WL 6743592, at *6–7 (C.D. Cal. July 7, 2020) (dismissing UCL unfairness

8     claim where the allegations of “unfairness” “rest solely in Plaintiffs’ breach of contract allega-

9     tions”).

10               The complaint’s threadbare UCL allegations add nothing to the breach of contract claim.

11    Plaintiff explicitly incorporates by reference its breach of contract allegations in its UCL claim,

12    and does not allege any facts suggesting any unfair conduct independent of the alleged breach. See

13    Compl. ¶ 81 (“By its conduct alleged herein, Facebook violated the “unfair” prong of the UCL by

14    overcharging advertising customers.”). Accordingly, the UCL claim does not extend beyond a

15    “garden-variety” breach of contract claim and should be dismissed for that reason alone. Rosell,

16    2014 WL 4063050, at *6 (dismissing UCL claim where plaintiffs failed to “allege a plus factor

17    showing an independent violation of the UCL, and have not come up with anything more than

18    breach of contract”).

19               Second, even if plaintiff’s UCL claim were not subject to dismissal as being duplicative of

20    the breach of contract claim, it fails on its own terms. All that plaintiff alleges regarding any

21    allegedly “unfair” business practice is that “Facebook’s conduct alleged herein is unethical, op-

22    pressive, and substantially injurious to Plaintiff and the Class.” Compl. ¶ 82. “[T]hese allegations

23    simply parrot the legal standard for ‘unfair business practice.’” Price v. Apple, Inc., 2022 WL

24    1032472, at *5 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 6, 2022) (dismissing UCL claim under “unfair” prong based on

25    identical allegations). The complaint “lacks any allegations that go towards comparing the harm

26    to consumers against the utility of [Facebook’s] conduct.” Williamson v. McAfee, Inc., 2014 WL

27    4220824, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 22, 2014) (dismissing UCL claim under “unfair” prong). Nor does

28    plaintiff “offer[] any case law or statutory analysis suggesting how the ‘unfair’ prong might apply

2     (N.D. Cal. May 22, 2023) (dismissing UCL claim). Plaintiff’s flimsy allegations that simply state

3     the legal standard fall far short of stating a UCL claim.

4             Third, plaintiff’s UCL claim fails under either test for unfairness used by California courts.

5     Taleshpour v. Apple Inc., 549 F. Supp. 3d 1033, 1045 (N.D. Cal. 2021), aff’d, 2022 WL 1577802

6     (9th Cir. May 19, 2022). To state a claim for unfairness under the UCL, a plaintiff must show

7     either (1) that the conduct is “tethered to specific constitutional, statutory, or regulatory provisions”

8     (the “tethering test”); or (2) that the harm to the consumer outweighs the utility of the defendant’s

9     conduct (the “balancing test”). See id. As to the tethering test, the complaint does not even attempt

10    to show that the UCL claim is “tethered” to any legislative policy. See, e.g., Holmes v. Hospira,

11    Inc., 2013 WL 12132046, at *7 (C.D. Cal. Jan. 10, 2013) (dismissing UCL unfairness claim and

12    explaining that “Plaintiff here has not alleged that the conduct is tethered to specific constitutional,

13    statutory, or regulatory provisions and therefore fails to satisfy the tethering test”).

14            As to the balancing test, because plaintiff’s theory for why Facebook’s conduct was “un-

15    fair” relies on the same allegations that support its breach of contract claim, plaintiff fails to state

16    a claim under this test for the same reason its breach of contract claim fails. See Millam v. Ener-

17    gizer Brands, LLC, 2024 WL 2988210, at *2 (9th Cir. June 14, 2024) (affirming dismissal of UCL

18    unfairness claim under balancing test because the alleged conduct was only supposedly wrongful

19    based on “the same rejected theory” underlying plaintiffs’ non-UCL claims).

20            In sum, plaintiff claims that it was “unfair” for Facebook to allegedly deviate from a “sec-

21    ond price” auction system, even though Facebook never promised the use of any particular auction

22    system to price advertisements. The UCL’s balancing test “does not authorize such broad and

23    limitless judicial intervention into private business affairs and transactions.” Gunn v. FCA US,

24    LLC, 2023 WL 5418736, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 22, 2023).

25            C.      Plaintiff’s Unjust Enrichment Claim Should Be Dismissed

26            Finally, plaintiff fails to state a claim for unjust enrichment. Even if plaintiff was permitted

27    under California law to bring standalone claims for unjust enrichment, such claims may not be

28    brought where an enforceable contract governs the parties’ relationship.

3     standalone cause of action for ‘unjust enrichment.’”). Plaintiff’s claim should be dismissed for

6     the unjust enrichment claim brought here is a quasi-contract claim that is precluded in light of

8     contract claim does not lie when an enforceable, binding agreement exists defining the rights of

9     the parties.”). The complaint expressly alleges the existence of an enforceable contract, as dis-

10    cussed above. But a plaintiff cannot allege an enforceable contract and simultaneously plead a

11    quasi-contract claim for unjust enrichment. See Saroya v. Univ. of Pac., 503 F. Supp. 3d 986,

12    998–99 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (dismissing unjust enrichment claim where plaintiff also “expressly al-

13    leges the existence of an enforceable agreement,” which “preclude[s] [plaintiff] from asserting a

14    quasi-contract claim under the theory of unjust enrichment”); see also Gardiner v. Walmart, Inc.,

15    2021 WL 4992539, at *8 (N.D. Cal. July 28, 2021) (dismissing unjust enrichment claim without

16    leave to amend and explaining that because “Plaintiff has expressly pleaded the existence of an

17    enforceable contract, he cannot bring a claim for unjust enrichment”).
